cards.explanation: The picture is servants watching their master's hand. The singer says, "As the eyes of servants look to the hand of their master…" (Psalm 123:2). Think of a busy kitchen where everybody's eyes are on the one hand that's about to point. Nobody's looking at their shoes, friends. Everybody's looking at that hand.

The answer is True! The singer doubles it up: "…as the eyes of a maidservant look to the hand of her mistress…" (Psalm 123:2). That's a second servant with her eyes on a second hand. Two pictures, one idea: these eyes stay locked in, and they aren't wandering off for a snack break.

They keep looking until He shows them mercy. The verse says their eyes are on the LORD their God "…until He shows us mercy." (Psalm 123:2). There's no timer on this one, friends. They keep looking until the mercy comes.

The word is contempt. The singer says, "Have mercy on us, O LORD, have mercy, for we have endured much contempt." (Psalm 123:3). The next verse says it comes "…from the arrogant…" and "…from the proud." (Psalm 123:4). Being looked down on like that is heavy, and I think that's why the asking is so loud.

The answer is False. Psalm 123 closes with "We have endured much scorn from the arrogant, much contempt from the proud." (Psalm 123:4). These verses show no answer from the LORD, and they never say the scorn stopped. The song ends on the asking, friends.

The word is Israel! David says, "If the LORD had not been on our side—let Israel now declare—" (Psalm 124:1). He's calling the whole nation to say it out loud together. That's a lot of voices for one sentence, friends.

The answer is True! David says that without the LORD on their side, "…they would have swallowed us alive…" (Psalm 124:3). He says it right after "…when their anger flared against us…" (Psalm 124:3). Notice it's a what-if, friends. He's telling what would have happened without the LORD on their side, and it's a scary picture.

The answer is False. Every flood line in this psalm is a "would have," like "…then the floods would have engulfed us… then the raging waters would have swept us away." (Psalm 124:4-5). David is telling what would have happened if the LORD had not been on their side (Psalm 124:1). Then he blesses the LORD, who "…has not given us as prey to their teeth." (Psalm 124:6).

What the LORD did not do is give them as prey to their teeth. David says, "Blessed be the LORD, who has not given us as prey to their teeth." (Psalm 124:6). Notice what he's thankful for, friends, something that didn't happen. That's a funny kind of gift, and it's a real one.

Israel escaped like a bird from the fowler's snare! David says, "We have escaped like a bird from the snare of the fowler…" (Psalm 124:7). A fowler is someone who traps birds. So the picture is a bird slipping out of the trapper's snare.
The answer is True! David says, "the net is torn, and we have slipped away." (Psalm 124:7). The trap is ripped, and the bird is out. That's one busted net, friends.

David says their help is in the name of the LORD. He ends with, "Our help is in the name of the LORD, the Maker of heaven and earth." (Psalm 124:8). After all those floods and nets, he lands on one place for help, friends. It's a good way to end a song.

The answer is True! The last line reads, "Our help is in the name of the LORD, the Maker of heaven and earth." (Psalm 124:8). Maker of heaven and earth, friends. Everything else in the song gets small next to that.
